findings: On 120 new episodes, K=1 and K=5 each succeed in 21/24 situations; K=10 succeeds in 20/24. K=5 uses 27.1 s mean compute versus 115.8 s for K=1. Their paired success differences from K=10 both include zero, so the shorter intervals cannot be reliably ranked or declared equivalent.

K=25 and K=50 succeed in 9/24 and 7/24 situations. Their paired differences from K=10 are -45.8 and -54.2 percentage points, with exploratory 95% intervals [-66.7, -25.0] and [-75.0, -33.3]. The relationship remains task-dependent and non-monotonic: drawer success is 0/8 at K=25 but 3/8 at K=50.

The pilot gave K=1 only 2/6 successes; it reaches 21/24 on the new states. Preserve that change in interpretation. Combined counts are 23, 26, 24, 11 and 9 out of 30 for increasing K, but the pooled result is supplementary because pilot outcomes motivated expansion.

Reviewed videos show an unrecovered can drop, a repeated bowl approach that still misses placement, and a successful drawer pull with fewer calls at K=50. Two state-2 drawer failures open the upper drawer instead of the middle one. Visible redirection and new observations do not guarantee recovery; contact-mechanism explanations remain hypotheses.

cases.title: A lost can is not recovered
cases.observation: K=10 retains the can during transport and reaches native success at step 139. K=25 lifts it, then loses it around steps 82-86 outside the basket. The hand continues toward the basket after replans at 100 and 125; it does not retrieve the can before the step-280 timeout.
cases.hypothesis: Slippage or contact geometry may explain the loss. A longer interval may leave fewer opportunities to adjust the grasp, but the recordings do not isolate the cause of the drop.
cases.evidence: Object/state3/seed11; both videos and review-object.json. Dense frames 76-94; gripper commands stay positive (0.987-1.000), so the loss is not a commanded release.

cases.title: A second approach still misses placement
cases.observation: K=50 withdraws at steps 80-100, returns at 105-125 after replan 100, transports the bowl at 130-160 and opens near the plate rim around 160. Placement remains incomplete at 280. K=1 succeeds at 80 using 80 calls; K=10 also succeeds at 75 using only 8 calls.
cases.hypothesis: A new plan can redirect an approach without ensuring accurate placement. The K=1 versus K=10 contrast shows that extra updates did not improve this binary outcome; it does not establish general equivalence.
cases.evidence: Spatial/state3/seed11; videos, steps/chunks and review-bowl.json. Replan 100 command jump 0.742472. Initial K=50 contact counts remain unknown.

cases.title: A longer plan opens the drawer sooner
cases.observation: Both episodes succeed. At K=5, the hand remains near the handle around steps 90-215 with little opening, then finishes at 252 after 51 calls. K=50 visibly pulls around 100-127 and succeeds at 127 after 3 calls. Measured compute time is 44.7 versus 4.9 seconds.
cases.hypothesis: A longer action sequence may sustain an effective pull in this state. Contact forces are not logged, so the delay at K=5 cannot be attributed uniquely to replanning.
cases.evidence: Goal/state3/seed11; matched initial-state and observation hashes; both videos, summary logs and review-drawer.json. Open-finger hooking is not a missed closing grasp.

conclusion: Replanning frequency changes both computational cost and task behavior. K=5 and K=10 offer useful observed cost-success compromises in this fixed setup, while the most frequent updates add substantial compute without exceeding K=5's validation success count. Longer intervals can work well in particular states despite lower aggregate success. No universal optimum follows from three tasks, eight new states per task and one policy seed. The intervals are exploratory and conditional; native success, assistant-only event annotation and synchronous simulation limit claims about stable placement, causal correction and real-time robots.
